caption:

The time to find out how someone handles a crisis is before the crisis, not during one.

SOME OF WHAT'S IN IT
· Panic is a choice. We stay calm because the next move is already written down.
· Contain, don't erase. Isolate the problem, but preserve the evidence — you will need to know what happened.
· Communicate out-of-band. Never discuss a live incident on a system that may be listening. Verify any payment change by voice.
· Recover from tested backups. An untested backup is not a backup; it's a hope.
· Blameless post-incident review. Every incident we handle makes the playbook better.
· A real person answers, 24/7, in-house — the same team you'd meet at 2 a.m.

The full playbook also covers the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle, our severity tiers, per-incident-type runbooks and the full communications protocol.

title: Wildfire Season: The Continuity Checklist | Pro Link Systems
caption:
Most Southern California businesses have a continuity plan.

Very few have ever run it.

Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them shows up on exactly one kind of day — the one where a public safety power shutoff arrives on schedule, announced days in advance, and completely outside your control.

What decides how that day goes isn't the size of the binder. It's whether anyone has opened it.

We made a 90-second film about the three things we check, in the order we check them:

1. Sequence. Not everything has to come back at once — but something has to come back first. Decide that before you need it, not at 7am in a dark office.

2. Location. A copy of what matters, somewhere the same outage can't reach.

3. Rehearsal. Run it on an ordinary Tuesday, when nothing is wrong.

The third one is the one everyone skips. It's also the only one that makes the first two real.

We've been doing this in Los Angeles since 1999. The checklist we use is free — link in the first comment.
